_: Devices seen in MORE THAN ONE film. A pattern is authored, not measured: it is what a person noticed after reading every sheet. Each cites the films it was seen in, so a reader can check it and so its weight is visible. One film is an idea; three is a technique. Rendered into engine-doctrine/CRAFT/GRAMMAR.md by `make grammar DOC=1`.

patterns.name: A beat is a BURST then a REST, never a constant rate
patterns.what: Inside one shot the change curve rises to a peak and then decays to near-nothing before the next beat arrives. It is not sustained motion; it is an event followed by silence.
patterns.why:
The per-frame curve of pin-583145851797705243 says it plainly. Shot 2 runs 3.9 · 2.4 · 2.5 · 5.7 · 2.1 · 1.6 · 0.9, shot 3 runs 4.7 · 8.1 · 6.6 · 7.1 · 5.9 · 2.7 · 0.8, and shot 5 sits at 1.1 · 1.5 · 0.6 for three quarters of a second before exploding to 18.4. Every shot ends quieter than its middle. The rest is what makes the next arrival read as an arrival, and the held share of 6 to 20% is where that rest shows up in the average.
THIS IS THE PATTERN I GOT BACKWARDS. Reading a low mean as the defect, I filled every flat segment of my own tracks with drift and produced a uniform churn: the number moved and the film got worse, because nothing landed. A mean is the wrong statistic for this entirely. The `curve` field exists so the SHAPE can be read, and the shape is what to copy.
patterns.ours: A keyed track that reaches its pose and then STOPS, with the next event starting later. Hold the pose with no keys rather than adding small ones to keep a number up. `idle` is the right amount of life for a rest: a 1.5% breath is below the still floor and does not fill the silence.

patterns.name: Blur-resolve as the entrance
patterns.what: Type arrives heavily motion-blurred and settles into focus. Nothing slides, fades or scales.
patterns.why: It reads as speed in a SINGLE FRAME, which a fade never does: a blurred still looks fast, a half-opacity still looks broken. Two of the three also use it to bracket the film, opening and closing on the same gesture.
patterns.ours: `motionAt` interpolates a `blur` channel, so this is one keyed track: [{t:0,blur:24},{t:0.4,blur:0}]. The `focusRack` blueprint does it and has zero users.

patterns.name: The ground inverts on every cut
patterns.what: Consecutive beats alternate dark and light, so no cut needs an effect on it.
patterns.why: The inversion IS the transition. `pin-72761350251141725` has no continuous object, no camera and no shared subject across seven shots, and still reads as one film purely because the ground alternates. `pin-333759022406800725` does it within a single hue, which is the gentler form.
patterns.ours: bg windows with no from/to bind to the joints in order (core/timeline/junctions.js), so the cuts own the numbers. 84% of our library paints ONE window for the whole runtime.

patterns.name: There are three ways to invert a frame, not one
patterns.what: The BACKDROP changes (rebuilt), the SUBJECT changes value (slabs go bright-on-black to dark-on-white), or the LIGHT changes over an unchanging world (80 seconds of black lit by blue, then orange, then white).
patterns.why: Only the first is a new world. The second reads as the same objects under different light; the third keeps the world identical and still gets the punctuation. We only ever reach for the first.
patterns.ours: The first is `bg` windows. The second is a rect or image whose colour is keyed. The third is a `glow` or `beam` layer, or an `adjust` layer grading everything beneath.

patterns.name: Hold the picture, move the type
patterns.what: Every photographic or rendered object is STILL. All the motion is type arriving and the ground changing.
patterns.why: It is what lets a film cut 33 times a minute without reading as frantic: the cut rate is high while the rate of change INSIDE a shot is low. `pin-924363892282992611` runs seven unrelated subjects in 19s and never feels busy.
patterns.ours: An `image` layer with no `ken` and no motion track, under text that carries the beat. We reflexively add a ken burns push and it costs us this.

patterns.name: One accent colour, one word at a time
patterns.what: Exactly one hue carries every emphasis in the film, and usually one word per beat wears it.
patterns.why: It tells the eye where to land in the 200ms a fast beat gives it. Measured in together-chat: the single accent holds 0.13% of all pixels and carries every emphasis in the film.
patterns.ours: The theme's `accent`, and nothing else. `designspec-check` already locks this; the discipline is using it on ONE word rather than on a whole line.

patterns.name: The loudest frame is often an absence
patterns.what: The peak measured frame is something LEAVING, or the frame flooding with flat colour, rather than something arriving.
patterns.why: It is the opposite reflex to ours. framer-hero is the counter-example where all four peaks are arrivals, so both work, but an emptying is available and we never use it.
patterns.ours: A keyed `exit` track (harness/author/track.mjs exit), or an `adjust`/rect flooding the frame for a few frames.

patterns.name: A container that holds while its contents change
patterns.what: One frame, pill, ring or window stays put and what is inside it swaps.
patterns.why: The cheapest continuity device in the store: the eye has somewhere to rest while the content changes, so a full swap does not read as a cut. arc-space-swiping recolours the container to match its new contents, which is the detail that makes it look designed.
patterns.ours: A `rect` or `group` that outlives its children's windows. It is also the honest way to pass `no-continuous-object`.

patterns.name: Escalate the unit, not just the pace
patterns.what: The film starts on single words at under a second and ends on sentences at four, so beat length and meaning grow together.
patterns.why: A pacing change that tracks the unit of meaning reads as structure. A pacing change on its own reads as arbitrary.
patterns.ours: Nothing stops this today; nothing suggests it either. It is a storyboard decision, not an engine feature.
